class_summary.evidence_analyzed: This public example preserves the grading/report structure while using fictional names and representative evidence patterns. Original student scans are not included.
strengths: Students generally identify the design goal and participate in iterative testing.
Most students can describe a plausible redesign.
Several students use measured test results when explaining performance.
needs: Use measurements consistently when comparing designs.
Connect the observed failure directly to the redesign.
Name tradeoffs instead of treating one redesign as simply “better.”
class_summary.highest_leverage_target: Make every redesign explanation follow evidence -> change -> expected effect.

class_summary.limitations: Public demonstration only. Student identities and original evidence scans were intentionally removed.

set1.label: Criteria and constraints
set1.prompt: A tower must be at least 40 cm tall and may use no more than 25 straws. Identify the criterion and the constraint.
set1.answer: Criterion: at least 40 cm tall. Constraint: no more than 25 straws.
set1.teacher_move: Ask students to underline what defines success and circle what limits the design.
set1.discourse_move: Compare how criteria and constraints play different roles in a design challenge.

set1.label: Fair testing
set1.prompt: Two tower designs are being compared. Name two conditions that should stay the same so the test is fair.
set1.answer: Examples: same materials, same table, same test time, same disturbance method.
set1.teacher_move: Press for variables that directly affect the comparison.
set1.discourse_move: Explain why changing several variables at once weakens the conclusion.

set1.label: Evidence
set1.prompt: Tower A stands 9 s and Tower B stands 27 s. Which design has stronger evidence of stability?
set1.answer: Tower B, because it remained standing 18 s longer.
set1.teacher_move: Require the number in the explanation.
set1.discourse_move: Compare a vague claim with an evidence-based claim.

set1.label: Failure analysis
set1.prompt: A tower repeatedly bends at the same joint before falling. What should the team investigate first?
set1.answer: The repeated weak joint and how it is connected/reinforced.
set1.teacher_move: Ask what the repeated pattern tells us about cause.
set1.discourse_move: Defend why the failure point is more useful than guessing a random redesign.

set1.label: Cause and effect
set1.prompt: Explain one reason a wider base can make a tall tower more stable.
set1.answer: A wider base increases support and makes tipping less likely by keeping the center of mass over the base for a larger range of tilt.
set1.teacher_move: Ask students to connect geometry to tipping.
set1.discourse_move: Use “because” to link the change to the effect.

set1.label: Redesign choice
set1.prompt: A tower is stable but too short. Which redesign best targets the problem: widen the base, increase height while preserving bracing, or add weight at the bottom?
set1.answer: Increase height while preserving bracing, because the unmet criterion is height.
set1.teacher_move: Ask which criterion is not yet met.
set1.discourse_move: Explain why the other changes do not directly solve the stated problem.

set1.label: Tradeoffs
set1.prompt: A redesign is taller but less stable. Explain the tradeoff and propose one next test.
set1.answer: The design improved height but reduced stability; next, test a bracing change while keeping height constant.
set1.teacher_move: Ask students to name both the gain and the cost.
set1.discourse_move: Compare redesigns that change one variable at a time.

set1.label: Evidence-based redesign
set1.prompt: A tower lasts 10 s, then 18 s after adding cross-bracing. What should the team conclude and test next?
set1.answer: Cross-bracing likely improved stability; repeat the test or vary bracing while holding other conditions constant.
set1.teacher_move: Ask what the data supports versus what it proves.
set1.discourse_move: Discuss why repeated trials strengthen the conclusion.

questions.prompt: A bridge must span 30 cm and use 15 sticks or fewer. Name the criterion and constraint.
questions.answer: Criterion: span 30 cm; constraint: 15 sticks or fewer.

questions.prompt: Why can a design meet a criterion but still fail the challenge?
questions.answer: It may violate a constraint or fail another criterion.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a material constraint.
questions.answer: Any valid limited-material example.

questions.prompt: Give one measurable success criterion for a tower.
questions.answer: Example: remain standing for 30 s.

questions.prompt: Why should two tower tests use the same table?
questions.answer: To keep testing conditions consistent.

questions.prompt: Name one variable to keep constant when testing base width.
questions.answer: Examples: height, materials, joint method.

questions.prompt: Why are repeated trials useful?
questions.answer: They reduce the chance that one unusual result controls the conclusion.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with changing base width and tower height at the same time?
questions.answer: You cannot tell which change caused the result.

questions.prompt: A lasts 12 s; B lasts 24 s. Which is more stable in this test?
questions.answer: B.

questions.prompt: What number should appear in a convincing comparison?
questions.answer: The measured test result(s).

questions.prompt: Is “it looked better” strong engineering evidence? Why not?
questions.answer: No; it is vague and not measurable.

questions.prompt: Turn “Design C was best” into an evidence-based statement.
questions.answer: A valid statement that cites measured data.

questions.prompt: A joint bends first every trial. What should be redesigned?
questions.answer: The joint/connection.

questions.prompt: A stable tower misses the height requirement. What should be targeted?
questions.answer: Height while preserving stability.

questions.prompt: Why is random redesign inefficient?
questions.answer: It may not address the actual failure or unmet criterion.

questions.prompt: Complete: The evidence shows ____, so we will change ____.
questions.answer: Any valid evidence-linked response.

questions.prompt: A wider base helps stability but uses more material. Name the tradeoff.
questions.answer: Stability versus material use.

questions.prompt: A taller tower meets height but tips sooner. What changed positively and negatively?
questions.answer: Height improved; stability decreased.

questions.prompt: Why should teams record tradeoffs?
questions.answer: To make informed decisions among criteria and constraints.

questions.prompt: Propose a next test for a tall but unstable tower.
questions.answer: A valid controlled test of bracing/base/support.

questions.prompt: A redesign improves time from 11 s to 20 s. What should happen next?
questions.answer: Repeat or test the specific change again while controlling other variables.

questions.prompt: What evidence would convince you a redesign works?
questions.answer: Consistent measured improvement across fair tests.

questions.prompt: Why is one successful trial not enough?
questions.answer: It may be due to chance or uncontrolled conditions.

questions.prompt: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement for a successful redesign.
questions.answer: Any valid CER using a measured result.
